title: Scalable entanglement distribution using encoded hybrid repeater chains
authors: Stav Haldar, Saikat Guha, Don Towsley, Filip Rozpędek
abstract: Long-distance entanglement distribution requires error correction protocols to compensate for qubit decoherence in quantum memories and noise introduced during entanglement swapping. We argue that repeater chains with error-correction capabilities should exploit more than one physical platform, combining the complementary strengths of different quantum memory technologies into a single hybrid repeater architecture. An important constituent of such an architecture is a hybrid repeater which combines type-1 memories, characterized by fast entanglement generation rates and suitability for multiplexing, and type-2 memories that offer long coherence times and low two-qubit gate error rates. Taking the resource-intensive nature of hybrid nodes into account, we propose and analyze repeater chains in which only a subset of nodes need to be hybrid, while the remaining nodes are simpler first-generation repeaters with no error-correction capability. Through detailed Monte Carlo simulations of fault-tolerant encoded repeater chain protocols based on the three-qubit phase-flip repetition code, the $[[7,1,3]]$ Steane code, and the $[[9,1,3]]$ Shor code, we demonstrate that these hybrid architectures outperform pure architectures based on a single memory platform in terms of end-to-end entanglement distribution rate. In our study we develop a full circuit-level noise model of our architectures and examine the impact of an imperfect interface between the two platforms on our hybrid architecture. We also develop a modified version of the swap-as-soon-as-possible policy with multiplexing, more suited to our architecture where some nodes perform error-correction while others do not. This modified policy significantly reduces the information storage time in memory qubits relative to the previously considered swap policies in encoded repeater chains.
summary: This paper proposes a novel hybrid repeater architecture for long-distance quantum communication, combining fast Type-1 memories with high-fidelity Type-2 memories. Through extensive simulations, the authors demonstrate that this hybrid approach significantly boosts the end-to-end entanglement distribution rate compared to using either memory type alone. This provides a crucial roadmap for building practical, fault-tolerant quantum networks.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving scalable, long-distance entanglement distribution by compensating for qubit decoherence and noise accumulated during entanglement swapping over repeater chains.
main_result: The proposed hybrid repeater architectures, which combine Type-1 and Type-2 quantum memories, significantly outperform pure architectures based on a single memory platform in terms of end-to-end entanglement distribution rate.
method: The authors use detailed Monte Carlo simulations to analyze fault-tolerant encoded repeater protocols, comparing performance across different memory combinations and optimized swapping policies.
model_or_system: The system models quantum repeater chains utilizing two types of quantum memories: Type-1 (fast generation, multiplexing) and Type-2 (long coherence, low gate error). Error correction is implemented using codes like the Steane and Shor codes.
key_observables: End-to-end entanglement distribution rate, logical error probabilities (perr,x, perr,y, perr,z), and the evolution of Bell state coefficients.
important_parameters: Gate error rates ($\epsilon_g$), coherence times ($T_2$), multiplexing capability ($\mu$), and the spacing between error-correcting nodes ($N_1$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that only a subset of nodes need to be the resource-intensive hybrid type, and it develops a modified swap-ASAP policy to optimize storage time.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the multiplexed repeater chain structure, the process of generating logical Bell pairs via local CNOTs and BSMs, and a comparison showing the performance advantage of the hybrid architecture over pure Type-1 or Type-2 chains.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need for hybrid repeaters, then details the simulation methodology using specific error-correcting codes (Steane, Shor), and finally presents the results demonstrating the rate enhancement and the optimization of the swapping policy.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the hardware limitations of quantum networking by proposing a resource-aware, hybrid architecture that maximizes entanglement distribution rates by strategically combining different physical memory platforms.
